title: Buffett on mistakes
lede: Buffett has reported his own errors to shareholders for five decades, itemising them by cause and putting a price on each. The record runs from the textile mills he should never have bought, through Dexter Shoe paid for in stock, to a tally of how often he says the word. It shows candour as a discipline, not a confession.

entries.excerpt: It is comforting to be in a business where some mistakes can be made and yet a quite satisfactory overall performance can be achieved. In a sense, this is the opposite case from our textile business where even very good management probably can average only modest results.
entries.note: Insurance mistakes survivable; textiles punish even good management. First framing of error tolerance by business quality.

entries.excerpt: By any statistical test, the purchase price was an extraordinary bargain; we bought well below the working capital of the business and, in effect, got very substantial amounts of machinery and real estate for less than nothing. But the purchase was a mistake.
entries.note: Waumbec, bought to expand textiles, reported as an error two years on; the turnaround lesson follows from it.

entries.excerpt: My own thinking has changed drastically from 35 years ago when I was taught to favor tangible assets and to shun businesses whose value depended largely upon economic Goodwill. This bias caused me to make many important business mistakes of omission, although relatively few of commission.
entries.note: First use of the omission and commission distinction; his own training named as the source of error.

entries.excerpt: We have tried to include all of our “rented suit” liabilities in our current financial statement, but our record of past error should make us humble, and you suspicious. I will continue to report to you the errors, plus or minus, that surface each year.
entries.note: Reserving errors had flattered results; he commits to publishing the annual loss-development figures to shareholders.

entries.excerpt: Any manager who consistently says “except for” and then reports on the lessons he has learned from his mistakes may be missing the only important lesson - namely, that the real mistake is not the act, but the actor.
entries.note: Year of the textile closure. Excuses excised: the manager, not the event, owns the miss.

entries.excerpt: My first mistake, of course, was in buying control of Berkshire. Though I knew its business - textile manufacturing - to be unpromising, I was enticed to buy because the price looked cheap.
entries.note: The twenty-five-year review starts with the company itself; a formal, listed retrospective becomes the reporting format.

entries.excerpt: Although I made an economic mistake in sticking with the textile business, I made no mistake in choosing Ken: He ran the operation well, he was always 100% straight with me about its problems, and he generated the funds that allowed us to diversify into insurance.
entries.note: Separates the economic error from the people decision; candour from a manager named as the saving grace.

entries.excerpt: Typically, our most egregious mistakes fall in the omission, rather than the commission, category. That may spare Charlie and me some embarrassment, since you don't see these errors; but their invisibility does not reduce their cost.
entries.note: The 1983 distinction reversed in weight; he starts volunteering errors shareholders could never have detected.

entries.excerpt: Agonizing over errors is a mistake. But acknowledging and analyzing them can be useful, though that practice is rare in corporate boardrooms. There, Charlie and I have almost never witnessed a candid post-mortem of a failed decision, particularly one involving an acquisition.
entries.note: Post-mortems named as rare boardroom practice; analysis of failure distinguished from agonising over it.

entries.excerpt: I’ve made three decisions relating to Dexter that have hurt you in a major way: (1) buying it in the first place; (2) paying for it with stock and (3) procrastinating when the need for changes in its operations was obvious.
entries.note: Dexter reported in a bad year for shoes; delay in acting treated as its own error, alongside price and currency.

entries.excerpt: And now it’s confession time. It should be noted that no consultant, board of directors or investment banker pushed me into the mistakes I will describe. In tennis parlance, they were all unforced errors.
entries.note: Ownership before the detail: no adviser or board to blame. Dexter later named his worst deal.

entries.excerpt: …I made some errors of omission, sucking my thumb when new facts came in that should have caused me to re-examine my thinking and promptly take action.
entries.note: Crisis year: omission reframed as failing to act on new facts, not merely failing to buy.

entries.excerpt: GAAP accounting, however, doesn’t come close to recording the magnitude of my error. The fact is that I gave Berkshire stock to the sellers of Dexter rather than cash, and the shares I used for the purchase are now worth about $5.7 billion.
entries.note: Fiftieth-anniversary letter: the accounts understate the Dexter loss; paying in shares is the real cost.

entries.excerpt: The final component in our GAAP figure – that ugly $11 billion write-down – is almost entirely the quantification of a mistake I made in 2016. That year, Berkshire purchased Precision Castparts (“PCC”), and I paid too much for the company.
entries.note: Precision Castparts: a write-down presented as the measured size of his own pricing mistake.

entries.excerpt: During the 2019-23 period, I have used the words “mistake” or “error” 16 times in my letters to you. Many other huge companies have never used either word over that span.
entries.note: Candour made countable: his own usage tallied against peers' silence, in his last annual letter.

entries.excerpt: My advice: Don’t beat yourself up over past mistakes – learn at least a little from them and move on. It is never too late to improve.
entries.note: Farewell note: learn from the error, then move on; the practice ends as advice rather than confession.
